title: California Lawmakers Create First Indian American Legislative Caucus
excerpt: The new caucus marks a historic step for the growing Indian diaspora community in the nation's most populous state, building on years of increasing political representation.
body:
• California state lawmakers have formed the first Indian American Legislative Caucus in the state's history, marking a milestone for the growing diaspora community.
  • Assemblymember Ash Kalra, the first Indian American elected to the California Legislature in 2016, is expected to play a central role in the caucus.
  • The caucus aims to address issues important to California's Indian American population, estimated at over 900,000 residents statewide.
  • The move follows the formation of similar identity-based caucuses in the Legislature, including the Native American, Black, Latino, and API caucuses.

A First for Indian Americans in Sacramento

California lawmakers have established the state's first Indian American Legislative Caucus, a historic step that reflects the growing political influence of one of the fastest-growing demographic groups in the United States, according to reports from the California state capital.

The formation of the caucus comes as Indian Americans have steadily increased their presence in California politics and civic life. The state is home to more than 900,000 Indian Americans, concentrated heavily in the San Francisco Bay Area, Silicon Valley, Los Angeles, and the Sacramento region, according to U.S. Census data.

"When I was first elected in 2016, I was the first Indian American to serve in the California Legislature. It's been a long time coming for our community to have a formal voice in the Capitol."

— Ash Kalra, California Assemblymember

Building on a Growing Political Presence

The caucus builds on years of incremental political gains by Indian Americans in California. Assemblymember Ash Kalra, who represents San Jose's 25th Assembly District, made history in 2016 as the first Indian American and first Hindu elected to the California State Legislature. He currently chairs the Assembly Judiciary Committee and is serving his fifth term.

While California has long had an Asian Pacific Islander Legislative Caucus — established in 2001 to represent the state's broad API community — advocates have argued that Indian Americans, with their distinct policy concerns around immigration, small business, and cultural preservation, needed dedicated representation in the statehouse.

The AAPI Legislative Caucus has been one of the largest in the Legislature, with more than a dozen members, but the new Indian American caucus would focus specifically on issues facing the South Asian diaspora, including H-1B visa policies, tech industry workforce concerns, and cultural engagement.

Reflects National Trend

The move mirrors a broader national trend. At the federal level, the Congressional Caucus on India and Indian Americans, co-chaired by Representatives Brad Sherman and Ro Khanna, has been one of the largest country-focused caucuses in Congress, with over 100 members across both parties in recent sessions.

Indian Americans have also seen growing representation at the state level across the country, with elected officials serving in legislatures in New Jersey, Texas, Georgia, and other states. California, with the largest Indian American population of any state, has been at the center of this political ascendancy.

The formation of the caucus also comes amid a wave of Indian American political firsts nationally. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whose mother emigrated from India, became the first person of Indian descent to hold either of the top two executive offices. Several Indian Americans now serve in Congress, including Representatives Ro Khanna and Raja Krishnamoorthi.

Policy Priorities

The caucus is expected to focus on several key areas relevant to California's Indian American community, including immigration reform, support for small businesses and tech entrepreneurs, educational access, addressing hate crimes targeting South Asians, and strengthening cultural ties between California and India.

California has historically been a leader in forming identity-based legislative caucuses. The Legislative Black Caucus, established in 1967, was the first, followed by the Latino Caucus in 1973. More recently, the state formed its Native American Legislative Caucus in 2021 after Assemblymember James Ramos became the first California Native American elected to the Legislature.

The Indian American caucus joins this growing ecosystem of caucuses that lawmakers say help amplify underrepresented voices and ensure diverse communities have a seat at the policy table in Sacramento.
